reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: An anorectal stricture is a fixed narrowing spanning the distal rectum and/or anal canal, more proximal and often more complex than isolated anal stenosis at the verge
Common causes include anastomotic strictures after low anterior resection or stapled anorectal surgery, radiation injury, Crohn disease, ischaemia, chronic inflammation, and neoplasia
Presentation includes obstructed defecation, tenesmus, narrow-calibre stool, straining, incomplete evacuation, and, when severe, features of large-bowel obstruction
A stricture with no clear benign explanation must be regarded as malignant until proven otherwise, and biopsy is mandatory
Anastomotic strictures after colorectal surgery are frequent, particularly after low stapled anastomoses, diverting stomas, or anastomotic leak, and many are short and web-like
Endoscopic assessment defines the level, length, and calibre, while cross-sectional imaging and examination under anaesthesia clarify complex or high strictures
Short benign strictures often respond to endoscopic or digital dilatation, whereas long, dense, radiation-related, or recurrent strictures may need stricturoplasty, resection, or diversion
Treatment must address the underlying disease, as strictures from Crohn disease or radiation behave differently from simple anastomotic scars
reference.pathophysiology: An anorectal stricture forms when the wall of the distal rectum or anal canal is narrowed by fibrosis, inflammation, ischaemia, or neoplastic infiltration, with loss of the normal distensibility of the lumen. After surgical anastomosis, ischaemia, subclinical leak, or scarring of the staple or suture line contracts the lumen into a fibrous ring. Radiation injury produces progressive obliterative endarteritis and submucosal fibrosis. Crohn disease drives transmural inflammation and fibrosis, and chronic infections or inflammatory dermatoses provoke cicatrisation. Malignant strictures narrow the lumen by mural infiltration. The rigid, non-compliant segment obstructs the passage of stool, causing straining, tenesmus, and proximal loading, and in tight strictures may progress to overt obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Rectal or anal carcinoma causing malignant stricture
Lymphogranuloma venereum or other infective stricture
Diverticular or extrinsic compressive narrowing of the distal bowel
additionalInvestigations: Endoscopy (rigid or flexible) to define level, length, and calibre and to obtain biopsies
Biopsy of the stricture to exclude malignancy and identify inflammatory causes
Examination under anaesthesia for complex, painful, or high strictures
Pelvic MRI or CT to assess mural and extramural extent
Contrast enema or defecography to characterise length and function
Assessment of anastomotic history, prior radiation, and inflammatory bowel disease status
redFlags: An irregular, ulcerated, or hard stricture suggesting malignancy
A stricture without a clear benign cause
Progressive obstruction with abdominal distension and vomiting
Rectal bleeding, weight loss, or a rising tumour marker
Associated fistula, abscess, or perianal Crohn disease
reference.prognosis: Short benign anorectal strictures often do well with dilatation, but long, dense, radiation-related, or recurrent strictures are more difficult and may require major surgery or permanent diversion; the outlook is dominated by the underlying cause, and malignant strictures carry the prognosis of the tumour.
pitfalls: Assuming a stricture is benign and omitting biopsy, thereby missing malignancy
Aggressive dilatation of dense or radiation strictures causing perforation
Failing to treat the underlying Crohn disease or radiation injury
Overlooking a subclinical anastomotic leak as the cause of a postoperative stricture
Repeated dilatation of a recurrent stricture without reassessing for underlying disease
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland guidance on benign and malignant anorectal disease
Standard coloproctology reference texts on anastomotic and radiation strictures
management: Biopsy every stricture without a clear benign explanation to exclude malignancy before treatment, and direct therapy at the underlying cause
Treat short benign strictures with endoscopic, digital, or bougie dilatation, repeated as required
Maintain luminal patency and ease passage with stool softeners and bulking agents
Manage refractory or complex benign strictures with stricturoplasty, advancement flap, or resection
Optimise medical therapy with immunosuppression or biologics in Crohn-related strictures, and dilate radiation strictures cautiously
Treat malignant strictures according to oncological staging and tumour type
Divert with a stoma for severe obstruction and refer to colorectal surgery for complex or high disease
